summary: For learners aged 12–14: interpret, convert and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is any integer. The central idea is that the exponent counts and directs the ×10/÷10 place-value shift — positive n for large numbers, negative n for small positive numbers — and that A must be kept in the range 1 ≤ A < 10 so each number has a unique form. For positive values, comparison is done by exponent first, then by A to break ties.
misconceptions: Miscounting the exponent — using the number of zeros incorrectly, or wrong sign for small numbers
Moving the digits the wrong direction for negative exponents (3.2×10⁻⁴ written as 32000)
Comparing by mantissa first and ignoring the exponent's dominance
Thinking a negative exponent makes the number negative rather than small/positive

activities.title: Dial-the-exponent place-value converter
steps: Set up two linked views: an ordinary number shown on a place-value chart, and an A × 10ⁿ expression you can change.

Starting with A = 4.5 and n = 0, increase n and watch the digits slide LEFT into higher place-value columns (equivalently, the decimal point moves right) one column per unit of n until 4.5 becomes 4,500,000 (4.5 × 10⁶); describe what each change of n does to the place value.

Now set A = 3.2 and n = −4; watch the digits slide RIGHT four columns into smaller place values (equivalently, the decimal point moves left four places) to give 0.00032, and state in words why the result is small but still positive.

Deliberately type an expression like 34 × 10⁵ and notice it is flagged as not in standard form; renormalise it yourself to 3.4 × 10⁶ by adjusting A and n together, then check the ordinary number is unchanged.
Record a short rule: 'n is how many places the point moves — right for positive n, left for negative n — and n never makes the number negative.'
activities.insight: Standard form is the ×10/÷10 place-value shift turned into notation: the exponent counts and directs how many columns the digits move, and a negative exponent makes a number small, not negative.

activities.title: Order standard-form numbers by scale
steps: Place 6.1 × 10⁵, 9.8 × 10⁴ and 2.3 × 10⁶ in order from smallest to largest; a magnitude scale strip can help you position them.
First decide the order by comparing exponents only (for these positive numbers, a bigger power means a bigger number), then use A only to break ties.
Test the trap directly: decide which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴; justify by exponent (5 beats 4) and confirm by converting to 320,000 vs 98,000.
Order 2 × 10³, 9 × 10² and 1.5 × 10³ and explain why 9 × 10² is smallest even though its coefficient 9 is the largest.
Write one sentence explaining your comparison method.
activities.insight: For positive numbers in standard form with A normalised to 1 ≤ A < 10, the exponent dominates the comparison; the mantissa A only matters when exponents are equal.

activities.title: Consolidate with two-way conversion checks
steps: Fill in the blank: 4,500,000 = ___ × 10ⁿ, keeping 1 ≤ A < 10 and stating n.
Convert 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to an ordinary number, resisting the tempting wrong answer of 32000.
Convert 47,000 and 0.0032 into standard form, then convert each answer back to check you land on the original number.
For every answer, verify by reversing the conversion so an off-by-one exponent is caught immediately.
activities.insight: Fluent two-way conversion, with a reverse-check habit, catches exponent miscounts and wrong-direction shifts.

activities.title: Argue about the negative exponent
steps: Respond to the challenge: 'Is 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ a negative number? Convince me.'
Explain, using 10⁻³ = 1/10³, why a negative exponent produces a small positive amount, not a negative value.
Contrast 10³, 10⁰ and 10⁻³ on a place-value scale to show how the exponent's sign controls size but never the sign of the number.
activities.insight: The sign of the exponent controls how large or small the number is, separately from whether the number itself is positive or negative.

activities.title: Ground standard form in real scales
steps: Examine an orders-of-magnitude scale (for example from a grain of sand to a galaxy, or atomic size to astronomical distance) and express several labelled quantities in standard form.
For each quantity, state whether n is positive or negative and what that tells you about the size.
Explain why standard form is useful for writing very large and very small quantities compactly.
activities.insight: Standard form is a practical tool for expressing and comparing quantities that span many orders of magnitude.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch the working: 'Write 47,000 in standard form. Write 0.0032 in standard form. Write 6.1 × 10⁻³ as an ordinary number. Then: which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴?' Watch the value of A they choose, how they treat the negative index, and how they compare.
